description_full: Owens Corning provides residential and commercial building products in the United States, Europe, the Asia Pacific, and internationally. It operates through three segments: Roofing, Insulation, and Doors. The company offers laminate and strip asphalt roofing shingles, roofing components, and oxidized asphalt. It also provides high, mid, and low temperature products; thermal and acoustical batts, loosefill insulation, spray foam insulation, wet use chopped strand, foam sheathing and accessories under the Owens Corning PINK, Next Gen, and FIBERGLAS Insulation brands; and glass fiber pipe insulation, energy efficient flexible duct media, bonded and granulated stone wool insulation, and cellular glass insulation and foam insulation under the FOAMULAR, FOAMGLAS, and Paroc brand names. In addition, the company offers residential interior and exterior doors; glass, fiberglass and metal, and door components such as frames, sills, weather-stripping, hinges and locks. Further, it manufactures, fabricates, and sells glass reinforcements in the form of fiber and mats. The company distributes its products to distributors, home centers and lumberyards, installers, retailers, homebuilders, contractors, dealers, building products retailers, and remodeling contractors. Owens Corning was incorporated in 1938 and is headquartered in Toledo, Ohio.

financial_summary: Owens Corning Inc is a mid-cap industrials business with a $9.4B market cap on $10.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 17% against a 8% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The business throws off $962M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
Accruals are elevated at -17.8% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 11.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 4% operating margin trails the Industrials median (9%) by 5pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.32x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 16% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 17% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 24% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 1.17, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $122.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 54% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 81% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $184, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 15%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $137 to $253 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 12.2 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 8.2 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 9.7 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 372% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 10.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 16 covering analysts target $143 on average, 18% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 8.1% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.81).
It runs a 23% gross margin and converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9, cash conversion of only -3.42x and high accruals (-17.8% of assets).
It spends 1.5% of revenue on R&D and 0.7% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.2x net debt to EBITDA ($345.0M of cash against $4.8B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.4x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.2% over 3 years, 7.4% over 5 years and 6.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 3.0% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 8.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 11.2% a year to shareholders (8.7% in buybacks and 2.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 5.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 104% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 25,000 employees, each generates about $404K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.8% a year.
That works out to $38K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.0M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
